name: (Dis-)Embedded Identification Scale
description: Four 5-item measures of collective identification examining how individuals identify with a subordinate ingroup and a superordinate (in)group: Embedded Identification (strong identification with both), Dis-Embedded Identification (strong subgroup ID, weak superordinate ID), Subordinate Ingroup Identification, and Superordinate (In)Group Identification. Items use configurable group-name placeholders. Validated in two samples (young Germans and Muslims in England). Bipolar −3 to +3 rating scale.
citation: Paffrath, J. (2024). The measurement of (dis-)embedded identification. Measurement Instruments for the Social Sciences, 6, Article e13783. https://doi.org/10.5964/miss.13783

name: 4D-Scale on Group Privileges (German)
description: German adaptation of the 20-item 4D-Scale (Shuman et al., 2024) measuring strategies used by White-identified individuals to manage awareness of racial privilege. Five subscales of 4 items each: Defend (justifying inequality), Deny (minimizing discrimination), Distance from Inequality (denying personal benefit), Distance from Identity (de-emphasizing White identity), and Dismantle (supporting systemic change). Validated across three German samples. Item 1 of Distance from Identity showed low factor loading in German and is not recommended for use in the German context.
citation:
Schröder, A.-C., & Asbrock, F. (2025). Managing a privileged group identity – Adaption and validation of a German 4D-Scale. Measurement Instruments for the Social Sciences, 7, Article e16079. https://doi.org/10.5964/miss.16079

Original scale: Shuman, E., Hasan-Aslih, S., van Zomeren, M., Saguy, T., & Halperin, E. (2024). The 4D-Scale: Measuring four orientations toward acknowledging group privileges. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/pspi0000449

name: Affirmative Character Scale
description: A 17-item scale measuring affirmative social character — adaptive authoritarian tendencies aligned with 21st-century meritocracy and flexible capitalism. Five subscales: Affirmation (3 items; uncritical acceptance of performance norms), Self-Optimization (5 items; self-discipline and self-tracking), Flexibility and Mobility (2 items; globalized adaptability), Solutionism (3 items; belief in technological fixes), and Libertarianism (4 items; market over state, entrepreneurial ideology). Note: the abstract states '28 items' but the final EFA-selected instrument comprises 17 items (confirmed in the Methods text). Validated in a German quota sample (N=1,196). Authors note the scale requires further refinement and revalidation. English translations of German items provided in the paper; no German verbatim reproduced.
citation: Jäger, D. W. G. F., Knasmüller, F., Brunner, M., & Heller, A. (2025). The affirmative character scale: A tool to explore new forms of authoritarianism. Measurement Instruments for the Social Sciences, 7, Article e16923. https://doi.org/10.5964/miss.16923

name: Big Five Inventory – Swahili Translation
description: Swahili translation of the 44-item Big Five Inventory (BFI; John et al., 1991), validated in a sample of 200 Kenyan university students at Pwani University. The translation covers all five Big Five dimensions: Extraversion, Agreeableness, Conscientiousness, Neuroticism, and Openness. Psychometric evaluation found low-to-moderate reliability (alpha .49–.73) and only partial replication of the five-factor structure; Conscientiousness and Neuroticism were best replicated. Full BFI with Swahili translation available in restricted/BFI/BFI.osd.
citation: Garrashi, H. H., Barelds, D. P. H., & De Raad, B. (2023). A psychometric evaluation of the Big Five Inventory (BFI) in an Eastern Africa population. Measurement Instruments for the Social Sciences, 5, Article e11207. https://doi.org/10.5964/miss.11207

name: Big Five Inventory-2 Extra-Short (PIAAC)
description: A 15-item ultra-brief measure of the Big Five personality domains (Extraversion, Agreeableness, Conscientiousness, Emotional Stability, Openness) developed for use in the Programme for the International Assessment of Adult Competencies (PIAAC). Three items per domain, one per facet. Available in 39 language versions across 40 countries.
citation: Rammstedt, B., Roemer, L., Behr, D., Bluemke, M., Lechner, C., Dept, S., Wäyrynen, L., Soto, C., & John, O. P. (2025). Going global: 39 language versions of the BFI-2-XS. Measurement Instruments for the Social Sciences, 7, Article e14067. https://doi.org/10.5964/miss.14067

name: Challenged Sense of Belonging Scale
description: A 4-item unidimensional scale measuring challenged (eroded) sense of belonging across four facets: Identification (no place in the world), Participation (not participating with others), Congruence (torn between worlds), and Connectedness (disconnected from those around). Validated in English, Arabic, and Farsi/Dari with refugee and asylum seeker samples in Germany (N=3,783). All items are negatively worded; higher scores indicate greater challenge to sense of belonging. NOTE: Response anchors run 1=Strongly agree to 5=Strongly disagree (reversed from typical convention).
citation: Fuchs, L. M., Jacobsen, J., Walther, L., Hahn, E., Ta, T. M. T., Bajbouj, M., & von Scheve, C. (2021). The Challenged Sense of Belonging Scale (CSBS)—A validation study in English, Arabic, and Farsi/Dari among refugees and asylum seekers in Germany. Measurement Instruments for the Social Sciences, 3, Article e11035. https://doi.org/10.1186/s42409-021-00021-y

name: Conspiracy Mentality Scale
description: An 11-item scale measuring general conspiracy mentality — the tendency to believe conspiracy theories — across two subscales: Conspiracy Theory Ideation (7 items) and Skepticism (4 items). Validated in French and Italian in this paper; English items published verbatim.
citation:
Stojanov, A., & Hannawa, A. (2023). Toward French and Italian language validations of the Conspiracy Mentality Scale (CMS). Measurement Instruments for the Social Sciences, 5, Article e11429. https://doi.org/10.5964/miss.11429

Original scale: Stojanov, A., & Halberstadt, J. (2019). Does lack of control lead to conspiracy beliefs? A meta-analysis. European Journal of Social Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1002/ejsp.2588

name: Democratic Values Scale for Children
description: A 22-item instrument measuring five democratic values in primary school children (grades 3–4, ages ~8–9): Participation (10 items), Equality (4 items), Following Rules (2 items), Renunciation of Violence (2 items), and Freedom of Opinion (4 items). Each subscale uses a distinct categorical response format; all items are dummy-coded (0/1) with the democratic response scored as 1. Validated in Germany (N=429). Equality, Following Rules, and Renunciation of Violence show strongest psychometric properties; Participation and Freedom of Opinion require further revision. Administered orally to children. German is the original language; English translations are provided in the paper.
citation: Monstadt, F. C. (2025). Measuring democratic values in primary school children: Development and confirmatory factor analysis of a new survey instrument. Measurement Instruments for the Social Sciences, 7, Article e16247. https://doi.org/10.5964/miss.16247

name: Duke University Religion Index
description: A 5-item index measuring religious involvement across two subscales: Religious Activity (ORA: organizational religious activity/attendance; NORA: non-organizational religious activity/private practice) and Intrinsic Religiosity (IR1–IR3: internalized religious motivation). Items use different response scales: ORA and NORA use 6-point frequency scales (0–5); IR items use a 5-point truth scale (1–5). Subscale scores are summed; higher scores indicate greater religious involvement. Originally validated in a US clinical population (Koenig et al. 1997). Psychometric properties in cross-cultural samples reported by Toscanelli et al. (2022).
citation: Toscanelli, C., Rezende, A. T., Pinto, J. M. de S., Branco, J. C., & Marques, L. F. (2022). Measurement of religiosity and spirituality: A cross-cultural validation study of the Duke University Religion Index (DUREL). Measurement Instruments for the Social Sciences, 4, Article e11133. https://doi.org/10.5964/miss.11133

name: Extended DCA-Transparency Scale – Short Version
description: A 10-item short version of the 20-item Extended DCA-Transparency Scale measuring perceived supervisor transparency across five dimensions: Disclosure, Clarity, Accuracy, Timeliness, and Relevance. Two items per dimension; each dimension scored as an unweighted mean. The referent ('supervisor') can be adapted to the specific context.
citation: Hossiep, C. R., Märtins, J., & Schewe, G. (2024). Measuring organizational transparency with 10 items: Validation of a German short scale. Measurement Instruments for the Social Sciences, 6, Article e11209. https://doi.org/10.5964/miss.11209

name: Four-Item Mentalising Index – German (FIMI-G)
description: A 4-item German translation of the Four-Item Mentalising Index (FIMI; Clutterbuck et al., 2021), measuring self-reported mentalising ability — the social-cognitive ability to understand and infer the non-emotional mental states of oneself and others. Unidimensional; higher scores indicate better mentalising ability. Item 2 is reverse-coded. German is the validated language; original English items are not reproduced here as the source (Clutterbuck et al., 2021) is not open access.
citation:
Bertrams, A., Blaise, M., & Krispenz, A. (2024). German translation of the Four-Item Mentalising Index (FIMI-G). Measurement Instruments for the Social Sciences, 6, Article e12249. https://doi.org/10.5964/miss.12249

Original scale: Clutterbuck, R. A., Callan, M. J., Taylor, E. C., Livingston, L. A., & Shah, P. (2021). Development and validation of the Four-Item Mentalising Index. Psychological Assessment, 33(7), 629–636. https://doi.org/10.1037/pas0001004

name: Fraboni Scale of Ageism – Short Form (Portuguese)
description: A 9-item Portuguese short form of the Fraboni Scale of Ageism (FSA; Fraboni et al., 1990), measuring the affective component of attitudes toward older adults across three subscales: Avoidance, Stereotypes, and Discrimination. Higher scores indicate greater ageism. Portuguese translation only — the original English FSA is copyrighted.
citation:
Neto, J., & Neto, F. (2024). Measuring ageism: Psychometric analysis of the Portuguese short form of the Fraboni Scale (FSA-SF). Measurement Instruments for the Social Sciences, 6, Article e11993. https://doi.org/10.5964/miss.11993

Original scale: Fraboni, M., Saltstone, R., & Hughes, S. (1990). The Fraboni Scale of Ageism (FSA): An attempt at a more precise measure of ageism. Canadian Journal on Aging, 9(1), 56–66. https://doi.org/10.1017/S0714980800016093

name: General Self-Efficacy Scale – Indian Adolescent Validation
description: Psychometric evaluation of Schwarzer & Jerusalem's 10-item General Self-Efficacy Scale (GSE) in Indian adolescents (N=2,601) from the Young Lives Survey. Factor analysis and MIRT revealed two dimensions: general self-efficacy (items 2,4,5,7,8,9,10) and task-specific self-efficacy (items 1,3,6). Cronbach's α = 0.75. Measurement invariance across sex confirmed. Full GSE OSD with 9 language translations is in restricted/GSE/GSE.osd. This MISS record tracks the Das et al. (2024) Indian adolescent validation publication; the full, runnable General Self-Efficacy Scale (GSE) — available in 32 languages — is in openscales/GSE.
citation: Das, S. K., Philip, M., Sudhir, P. M., & VS, B. (2024). Psychometric evaluation of Schwarzer & Jerusalem's General Self-Efficacy Scale among Indian adolescents: A factor analysis and multidimensional item response theory approach. Measurement Instruments for the Social Sciences, 6, Article e13651. https://doi.org/10.5964/miss.13651

name: Hate Crime Beliefs Scale – Universal
description: A 13-item context-independent scale measuring attitudes toward hate crime across three dimensions: Denial (8 items; minimizing the significance of hate crime), Sentencing (3 items; support for enhanced penalties), and Compassion (2 items; concern for victims). Developed and validated in German and English across three pre-registered studies (Germany and U.S.). Higher Denial scores indicate greater minimization; higher Sentencing and Compassion scores indicate more supportive attitudes toward hate crime recognition.
citation: Bender, R., Wagner, D., & Asbrock, F. (2025). Assessing attitudes towards hate crime: Adaptation and validation of the Hate Crime Beliefs Scale. Measurement Instruments for the Social Sciences, 7, Article e16239. https://doi.org/10.5964/miss.16239

name: International Survey Attitude Scale
description: A 9-item scale measuring attitudes toward surveys across three subscales: Survey Enjoyment (3 items; intrinsic interest in surveys), Survey Value (3 items; perceived societal importance), and Survey Burden (3 items; perceived intrusiveness and effort). Validated in English, Dutch, and German samples with measurement equivalence. One Value item (V3) and all three Burden items are negatively worded. Authors recommend using subscales separately rather than a single total score.
citation: de Leeuw, E., Hox, J., Silber, H., Struminskaya, B., & Vis, C. (2019). Development of an International Survey Attitude Scale: Measurement equivalence, reliability, and predictive validity. Measurement Instruments for the Social Sciences, 1, Article e11011. https://doi.org/10.1186/s42409-019-0012-x

name: Interpersonal Trust Short Scale (English Adaptation)
description: A 3-item unidimensional ultra-short scale measuring interpersonal trust as a psychological disposition — the general tendency to believe that other people have good intentions. Adapted into English from the German KUSIV3. Item 2 is reverse-coded. Validated in English-speaking samples. Higher scores indicate greater interpersonal trust. Completion time approximately 30 seconds.
citation: Nießen, D., Beierlein, C., Rammstedt, B., & Lechner, C. M. (2020). An English-language adaptation of the Interpersonal Trust Short Scale (KUSIV3). Measurement Instruments for the Social Sciences, 2, Article e11019. https://doi.org/10.1186/s42409-020-00016-1

name: Metacognitive Prospective Memory Inventory – Short Version
description: A 22-item short form of the Metacognitive Prospective Memory Inventory measuring self-reported prospective memory (PM) across three subscales: Prospective Memory Abilities (PMA, 8 items), Internal PM Strategies (PMSi, 7 items; mental/cognitive strategies), and External PM Strategies (PMSe, 7 items; external aids). 5-point frequency scale. Higher PMA scores indicate better PM abilities; higher PMSi and PMSe scores indicate more frequent strategy use. Validated in German with English translations provided in paper. Age-specific reference data recommended.
citation: Rummel, J., Danner, D., & Kuhlmann, B. G. (2019). The short version of the Metacognitive Prospective Memory Inventory (MPMI-s): Factor structure, reliability, validity, and reference data. Measurement Instruments for the Social Sciences, 1, Article e10999. https://doi.org/10.1186/s42409-019-0008-6

name: Modern Comprehensive F Scale
description: A 9-item unidimensional scale measuring authoritarianism, integrating all nine facets of the California F Scale (Adorno et al., 1950): Anti-intraception, Superstition and Stereotypy, Power and Toughness, Destructiveness and Cynicism, Projectivity, Sexuality and Gender Roles, Authoritarian Aggression, Authoritarian Submission, and Conventionalism. Validated in Germany (N=469) and the U.S. (N=314) with good reliability (ω=.87/.90). Three items are reverse-coded. Higher scores indicate greater authoritarianism.
citation:
Sorrentino, A., Prott, K., Hoffmann, L., Heidemeyer, P., Grau, I., & Banse, R. (2025). A new measure of authoritarianism: Development and validation of the Short Modern Comprehensive F Scale in Germany and the U.S. Measurement Instruments for the Social Sciences, 7, Article e16537. https://doi.org/10.5964/miss.16537

Original scale: Adorno, T. W., Frenkel-Brunswik, E., Levinson, D. J., & Sanford, R. N. (1950). The authoritarian personality. Harper.

name: Momentary-Chronic Regulatory Focus Scale
description: A 16-item state/trait scale measuring regulatory focus theory constructs across four subscales: Ideals focus (Id; 4 items), Oughts focus (Ou; 4 items), Gain focus (G; 4 items), and Non-Loss focus (N-L; 4 items). Items use a flexible stem allowing temporal or domain specificity (e.g., 'at this moment', 'today', 'at work'). All 16 items use a 7-point scale (1=does not apply at all to 7=applies fully). An 8-item abbreviated version (marked with superscript a) uses items Id1, Id4, Ou1, Ou3, G1, G2, N-L1, N-L3. Validated for momentary (state) and chronic (trait) measurement. Developed in English and German.
citation: Fay, D., Urbach, T., & Scheithauer, M. (2019). The Momentary-Chronic Regulatory Focus scale. Measurement Instruments for the Social Sciences, 1, Article e10993. https://doi.org/10.5964/miss.10993

name: Multidimensional Scale of Perceived Social Support – Igbo Translation
description: Igbo translation and psychometric evaluation of the 12-item Multidimensional Scale of Perceived Social Support (MSPSS; Zimet et al., 1988). Validated in a sample of 504 Igbo-speaking Nigerian undergraduate students. Confirmatory factor analysis supported a three-factor structure (Significant Other, Family, Friends) with adequate fit indices and acceptable reliability (alphas .71–.82). Full MSPSS OSD with English and Igbo translations is in restricted/MSPSS/MSPSS.osd.
citation: Iorfa, S. K., Ottu, I. F. A., Oguntayo, R., Ayandele, O., Kolawole, S. O., Gandi, J. C., Dangiwa, A. L., & Olapegba, P. O. (2020). COVID-19 knowledge, risk perception and precautionary behavior among Nigerians: A moderated mediation approach. Frontiers in Psychology, 11, 566773. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2020.566773

name: Nuclear Weapons Knowledge Scale
description: A 10-item objective knowledge test measuring public factual knowledge about nuclear weapons. Items cover nuclear-armed states (6 items: USA, Russia, China, India, Pakistan, Israel), cities bombed with atomic weapons in World War 2 (2 items: Hiroshima, Nagasaki), and immediate effects of a nuclear detonation (2 items: fire, blast). All items are binary-scored (1=correct, 0=incorrect). Total score range 0–10; higher = greater knowledge. Validated in 8-country European/American sample.
citation: Fialho, F. A. S. (2021). Public knowledge about nuclear weapons: A cross-national measure. Measurement Instruments for the Social Sciences, 3, Article e11063. https://doi.org/10.5964/miss.11063

name: Optimism–Pessimism Short Scale–2 (English Adaptation)
description: A 2-item ultra-short scale measuring dispositional optimism–pessimism. Item 1 assesses optimism, item 2 assesses pessimism (reverse-coded). Each item begins with a brief definition of the construct to ensure shared understanding. Validated in English (UK) and German samples with scalar measurement invariance. Higher scores indicate greater dispositional optimism. Completion time approximately 20 seconds.
citation: Nießen, D., Groskurth, K., Kemper, C. J., Rammstedt, B., & Lechner, C. M. (2022). The Optimism–Pessimism Short Scale–2 (SOP2): A comprehensive validation of the English-language adaptation. Measurement Instruments for the Social Sciences, 4, Article e11067. https://doi.org/10.1186/s42409-021-00027-6

name: Perceived Political Self-Efficacy Scale
description: A 10-item unidimensional scale (with validated 4-item short form) measuring perceived political self-efficacy — confidence in one's ability to execute political actions ranging from expressing opinions to mobilizing others and monitoring elected officials. Adapted into English from Italian (Caprara et al., 2009) and validated against German translation. No reverse-coded items. Higher scores indicate greater perceived political self-efficacy. A 4-item short form (items 3, 4, 8, 10) is also validated.
citation:
Bromme, L., Rothmund, T., & Caprara, G. V. (2020). A translation and validation of the Perceived Political Self-Efficacy (P-PSE) Scale for the use in German samples. Measurement Instruments for the Social Sciences, 2, Article e11013. https://doi.org/10.1186/s42409-020-00013-4

Original scale: Caprara, G. V., Vecchione, M., Capanna, C., & Mebane, M. (2009). Perceived political self-efficacy: Theory, assessment, and applications. European Journal of Social Psychology, 39(6), 1002–1020. https://doi.org/10.1002/ejsp.604

name: Political Efficacy Short Scale (English Adaptation)
description: A 4-item scale measuring political efficacy across two subscales: Internal Political Efficacy (2 items; belief in one's own political competence) and External Political Efficacy (2 items; belief in the responsiveness of political institutions). Adapted into English from the German PEKS (Beierlein et al., 2014). Validated in UK and German samples. No reverse-coded items. Higher scores indicate greater perceived political efficacy.
citation: Groskurth, K., Nießen, D., Rammstedt, B., & Lechner, C. M. (2021). An English-language adaptation and validation of the Political Efficacy Short Scale (PESS). Measurement Instruments for the Social Sciences, 3, Article e11031. https://doi.org/10.1186/s42409-020-00018-z

name: Porto Saudade Scale
description: A 5-item unidimensional scale measuring saudade proneness — the frequency with which an individual experiences saudade (a Portuguese emotional concept of longing for absent people, places, or things). Items 1–3 and 5 use a 7-point frequency scale; item 4 uses a 7-category ordered frequency format. Developed and validated in Portuguese adolescents and Brazilian international students. Higher scores indicate greater saudade proneness.
citation: Neto, F. (2021). Psychometric properties of the Porto Saudade Scale. Measurement Instruments for the Social Sciences, 3, Article e11049. https://doi.org/10.1186/s42409-021-00022-x

name: Quadrangular Love Scale – Cross-Cultural Validation
description: Cross-cultural psychometric study of the 40-item Quadrangular Love Scale (QLS; Karandashev & Evans, 2019) across Australian and Chinese samples. Confirmed four-factor structure (Compassion, Affection, Closeness, Commitment) with measurement invariance across cultures. Full QLS OSD is in restricted/QLS/QLS.osd.
citation: Karandashev, V., Evans, N. D., Zarubko, E., & Dorokhova, T. (2021). Cross-cultural comparison of the Quadrangular Love Scale: Measurement invariance across Australian and Chinese samples. Measurement Instruments for the Social Sciences, 3, Article e11077. https://doi.org/10.5964/miss.11077

name: Relationship Disillusionment Scale – Short Form
description: A 3-item unidimensional short form of the Relationship Disillusionment Scale (RDS), measuring the perception that one's romantic relationship is not meeting expectations and getting worse, and that one views one's partner increasingly negatively. Each item represents one of three core disillusionment facets: perceived deterioration, disappointment, and reduced positive regard. Developed and validated across three U.S. datasets; performs comparably to full-length RDS versions (11+ items). Higher scores indicate greater relationship disillusionment.
citation: Dover, C. R., Reifman, A., Rezvani Shakib, M., Pickett, A. S. M., Oldham, C. R., & Niehuis, S. (2026). Shortening the Relationship Disillusionment Scale to a Three-Item Measure (RDS-3). Measurement Instruments for the Social Sciences, 8, Article e20841. https://doi.org/10.5964/miss.20841

name: Right-Wing Extremist Attitudes Scale
description: An 18-item scale measuring right-wing extremist attitudes across six theoretically grounded subdimensions: Support for a Right-Wing Dictatorship (F1; REX01, REX03, REX04), National Chauvinism (F2; REX08, REX12, REX14), Trivialization of National Socialism (F3; REX02, REX11, REX18), Xenophobia (F4; REX06, REX10, REX16), Antisemitism (F5; REX07, REX13, REX17), and Social Darwinism (F6; REX05, REX09, REX15). Items use a 5-point Likert scale (1=fully disagree to 5=fully agree). Validated across five repeated cross-sectional German population surveys (Mitte-survey, 2014–2023) confirming a stable second-order factor structure with measurement invariance over time and demographic subgroups. Originally developed in German; English translation from Heller et al. (2022). The scale has been in use in Germany for over 20 years.
citation: Küpper, B., Reinecke, J., Mokros, N., & Zick, A. (2025). Validation of a model of right-wing extremist attitudes based on a repeated cross-sectional survey in Germany. Measurement Instruments for the Social Sciences, 7, Article e16909. https://doi.org/10.5964/miss.16909

name: Self-Appraisal of Masking Instrument
description: A 5-item instrument measuring self-appraisals of wearing a face mask during the COVID-19 pandemic. Two versions: Prospective (how respondents think they would feel wearing a mask) and Retrospective (how they did feel). Items cover pride in contributing to public health, self-consciousness about being judged, feeling silly, fear of being perceived as dangerous, and concern about racist aggression. Items are NOT intended to be summed into a composite score — each captures a distinct self-appraisal consideration. Validated in the USA in English only. Predictive validity demonstrated: prospective masking emotions predicted voting behavior 27 weeks later.
citation: Block Jr., R., & Plutzer, E. (2022). The Self-Appraisal of Masking Instrument. Measurement Instruments for the Social Sciences, 4(1), Article e11071. https://doi.org/10.1186/s42409-022-00032-3

name: Self-Compassion Scale – Preadolescent
description: Two scales of self-compassion for preadolescents aged 9–12, modelled on Neff's Self-Compassion Scale. The self-report version (SCS-P, 25 items) is completed by the child; the parent-report version (SCS-P-PR, 24 items) is completed by a parent about the child. Both yield two subscales: Compassionate Self-Responding (CSR) and Uncompassionate Self-Responding (USR). The version is selected via the 'respondent' parameter.
citation: Barclay-Timmis, V. S., Burton, L. J., & Beccaria, G. (2023). The development and psychometric evaluation of two new scales of self-compassion for preadolescents. Measurement Instruments for the Social Sciences, 5, Article e11199. https://doi.org/10.5964/miss.11199

name: Social Desirability–Gamma Short Scale (English Adaptation)
description: A 6-item short scale measuring social desirability across two subscales: PQ+ (Exaggerating Positive Qualities, 3 items) and NQ− (Minimizing Negative Qualities, 3 items). Adapted into English from the German KSE-G (Kemper et al., 2014). Validated in English-speaking samples. Higher PQ+ scores indicate greater tendency to claim positive attributes; higher NQ− scores indicate greater tendency to deny negative behaviors.
citation: Nießen, D., Partsch, M. V., Kemper, C. J., & Rammstedt, B. (2019). An English-language adaptation of the Social Desirability–Gamma Short Scale (KSE-G). Measurement Instruments for the Social Sciences, 1, Article e10985. https://doi.org/10.1186/s42409-018-0005-1

name: Tolerance for Ambiguity Scale – German Version
description: German translation of the 12-item Tolerance for Ambiguity Scale (TAS; Herman et al., 2010), validated in a three-wave online panel study in Germany (n = 1,370). Measures the ability to deal with ambiguous stimuli or situations across four sub-dimensions: Valuing Diverse Others, Change, Challenging Perspectives, and Unfamiliarity. Higher scores indicate greater tolerance for ambiguity. Reverse-coded items reflect intolerance.
citation:
Lietz, A. (2023). Measuring tolerance for ambiguity: A German-language adaption and validation of the Tolerance for Ambiguity Scale (TAS). Measurement Instruments for the Social Sciences, 5, Article e11211. https://doi.org/10.5964/miss.11211

Original scale: Herman, J. L., Stevens, M. J., Bird, A., Mendenhall, M., & Oddou, G. (2010). The tolerance for ambiguity scale: Towards a more refined measure for international management research. International Journal of Intercultural Relations, 34(1), 58–65. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ijintrel.2009.09.004

name: Trust in Science Short Scale
description: A 4-item unidimensional short scale measuring trust in science and scientists, developed from the Trust in Science and Scientists Inventory (Nadelson et al., 2014). Validated in adults (N = 449) and adolescents aged ~13+ (N = 298 parent-adolescent dyads) with excellent model fit, reliability (ω = .835), and measurement invariance across gender and age. Higher scores indicate greater trust in science.
citation:
Steger, D., & Schütz, A. (2025). Assessing trust in science: Development and validation of a short scale for adolescents and adults. Measurement Instruments for the Social Sciences, 7, Article e16225. https://doi.org/10.5964/miss.16225

Original item source: Nadelson, L., Jorcyk, C., Yang, D., Jarratt Smith, M., Matson, S., Cornell, K., & Husting, V. (2014). I just don't trust them: The development and validation of an assessment instrument to measure trust in science and scientists. School Science and Mathematics, 114(2), 76–86. https://doi.org/10.1111/ssm.12051
